A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and support a complete comparison. V1's methods, experiments and limitations can be matched to v2's main text and Appendices A-L; no material reading gaps remain.

before.justification: V1 reports original face-recognition training results, benchmark comparisons, parameter ablations and sampling-runtime experiments.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds generation runtimes, demographic evaluation on RFW and direct leakage analyses.

M1.justification: The specified latent prior changes from N(1,I) in v1 Equation 7 to N(0,I) in v2 Section 3.2. Otherwise, Langevin, Dispersion and DisCo retain their losses and update procedures. Appendix H explicitly formulates training-set repulsion already described and tested in v1 Section 4.6; it is not a new component.

E1.justification: V2 adds RFW evaluation covering Caucasian, Asian, Indian and African groups, extending demographic coverage within face verification. The existing seven recognition benchmarks remain; IJB-B and IJB-C results move to Appendix K.

E2.justification: The comparator sets in Table 1, the ROC plots and the Langevin-versus-Reject experiment are retained. RFW uses previously evaluated comparison methods. Appendix H illustrates the DCFace leakage comparison already discussed in v1 Section 4.6.

E3.justification: Table 1 revises reported sample counts: Syn-Multi-PIE changes from 1,800,000 to 180,000 images, and the 30,000-identity DisCo dataset from 1,650,000 to 1,950,000. Unchanged accuracies do not establish reruns. V2 also introduces protocols for subgroup evaluation, all-pair leakage matching with nearest-pair inspection, and GPU timing; established recognition-training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 substantially expands analysis of computational cost, demographic disparities and privacy. Appendix D adds runtime scaling, Appendix H adds synthetic-to-training distance distributions and nearest-image comparisons, and Appendix J evaluates demographic performance. Existing parameter sweeps, erosion analysis and dataset-scaling ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Table 13 newly reports standard deviations described as variation across demographic-group accuracies. This adds statistical dispersion reporting, not uncertainty across repeated training runs. Neither version supplies training-seed counts, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Legacy accuracy entries and ROC findings are retained, while substantial new result families appear. These include generation runtimes, leakage-distance plots and image comparisons, and RFW results: Langevin-DisCo-1.6M reports 84.74% average accuracy versus 85.27% for DCFace-1.2M. These are additional evaluations, not improvements over v1 under matched settings.

T1.justification: V2 Section 3.1 adds an equilibrium-distribution assumption and a Fokker-Planck formulation connecting distribution evolution to particle dynamics. Appendix D adds asymptotic complexity analysis. The existing optimization equations largely remain, and no convergence theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The three algorithmic contributions and competitive-performance claims remain. However, the abstract strengthens v1's statement that the method can mitigate leakage into the assertion that it prevents leakage, substantively strengthening the claimed privacy outcome.

C2.justification: V2 describes stochastic noise as optional, reports no observed jamming and suggests a small convergence benefit. Appendix H qualifies the assessment of leakage in its own dataset and notes difficulty comparing children. Appendix J adds a lowest-bias interpretation. Existing reference-model bias and computational-cost limitations remain in Appendix L.

D1.justification: V2 replaces v1's pending-URL placeholder with a concrete project-page address and states that code and datasets are public. Appendix D adds NVIDIA RTX 3090 hardware, a forward-pass batch size of 64, timing conditions and resource requirements. Existing hyperparameter defaults remain, although the earlier bob-package pointer is removed.

R1.justification: V2 removes much of the broad review of GAN architectures, inversion, diffusion and 3D modeling, concentrating on synthetic recognition datasets. It adds directly relevant positioning against repulsive MMD-GAN losses, Coulomb GANs and generative particle models, alongside demographic-bias and specific synthetic-identity-leakage research.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, physics motivation and conclusion are substantially rewritten or condensed. Extensive experimental material and future directions move into Appendices A-L, with new explanatory sections and an impact statement. This is a substantial narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: V2 adds synthetic-image galleries, leakage-distance plots, nearest-image comparison panels, runtime tables and an RFW table. Existing diagrams, plots and tables are extensively relocated and resized within a conference layout and single-column appendices; their relocation does not constitute new results.

improvement.justification: V2 improves reproducibility documentation and adds useful cost, privacy and demographic evidence. However, its stronger leakage-prevention claim conflicts with Appendix H's inconclusive assessment. The new lowest-bias conclusion also relies on inconsistent statistics: Table 13's own-method accuracies yield a population standard deviation of about 2.93, not the reported 1.81; DigiFace's displayed scores yield about 2.54. These weaknesses undermine the added ethical assurances, making the net quality effect uncertain despite clear documentation gains.
